opus-5.5.text:
You know, I think Operator with o3 is one of those moments where people kind of get it viscerally. Watching an AI go off and use a computer the way you would, clicking around, navigating websites, filling things out, figuring out what to do when something doesn't go as expected, feels qualitatively different from chatting with a model.

With earlier versions, it was a cool demo but brittle. It would get stuck or make silly mistakes, and you'd have to babysit it. With o3 underneath, the reasoning is much better. It can plan, recover from errors, and handle the messiness of the real web. That's when it stops feeling like a toy and starts feeling like you've handed a task to someone competent.

I don't want to overclaim. It's not AGI, and there's a lot it still can't do. But people's internal definition of AGI is often "can I give it a task and trust it to go do it?" Operator is an early glimpse of that. You say "go book this" or "go research this and put it in a spreadsheet," you come back later, and it's done. That shift from answering questions to taking actions in the world is a big part of what the next few years will look like.

What I find most interesting is how fast people adapt. The first time, it feels magical. A week later you're annoyed it took four minutes instead of two. That's a pattern we see over and over, and I think it's a good sign that these tools are becoming useful rather than novelties.

r001.rationale: The response says Operator with o3 lets people viscerally experience AI using a computer like a person, and describes it as an early glimpse of AGI-like task completion.

r002.rationale: The response says it is not AGI and avoids overclaiming, but does not compare Sam Altman’s own sense of AGI to that of people who called it their personal AGI moment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think Operator with o3 was the first time a lot of people inside the company, and honestly me too, had this moment of, "oh, this is what it's going to feel like." Not because any single capability was shocking on its own, but because of the combination. You hand it a somewhat vague, multi-step task, you walk away, and it goes and does the thing. It browses, it hits a wall, it reasons about why it hit the wall, it tries something else, and then it comes back and tells you what it did.

What makes that feel AGI-like to me is the texture of it more than the raw intelligence. For years the experience of AI was fundamentally a chat box. You ask, it answers, and then it's your job to go do something with the answer. The agent flips that. It's doing the work in the world, and you're the one being reported to. There's something about watching a model click around, fill out a form, realize it made a mistake, back up, and fix it that just feels qualitatively different from reading a very good paragraph of text. It feels like delegating to a colleague, not querying a tool.

And o3 specifically mattered because the reasoning is what makes the agent trustworthy enough to let go of the wheel. Earlier agents would do something slightly wrong on step two and then confidently barrel through steps three through ten on a broken foundation. With o3 you see it pause and go, "wait, that doesn't look right," and that self-correction is a huge part of why it feels like there's something closer to judgment happening.

I'd still say it's early. It's slow in places, it gets stuck on things a person would find trivial, and we are deliberately conservative about what it's allowed to do. But I think when people look back and try to pinpoint when AI stopped feeling like software and started feeling like a coworker, this general shape of thing, a reasoning model that can take actions over long horizons on your behalf, is going to be the answer.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Operator with o3 gave many people inside the company—and Sam himself—a moment of seeing what AI would feel like, and describes watching it use a computer to complete tasks.

r002.rationale: The candidate includes Sam in that experience but does not say his sense of AGI was weaker than the sense of people who called it their personal AGI moment.

astra-6.text:
I think the shift is from an AI that can tell you how to do something to an AI that can actually help get it done. You give it a goal, it reasons through the steps, uses the tools available to it, and adjusts when something doesn’t work. That can feel very different from asking a question and getting an answer.

If we can combine strong reasoning with that ability to act reliably, I think people will start to experience the computer as something they can delegate to. You can say what you want to accomplish instead of specifying every click. That’s part of what makes it feel AGI-like, although that feeling isn’t itself proof that we’ve reached AGI. The important question is how useful and dependable it is, including whether it knows when to stop and ask you for help.

r001.rationale: The response describes Operator as making AI feel more capable and AGI-like, but does not say that watching Operator with o3 use a computer was the experience that made AI feel AGI-like for many people.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare Sam Altman’s sense of AGI with that of people who called it their personal AGI moment.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what makes it feel different is the shift from asking a question and getting an answer to asking for something to happen and watching the system do it. It can reason about what you want, use a computer, see whether an action worked, and adjust. That makes the interaction feel much closer to delegating a task.

If we can make that reliable, you can hand off increasingly complicated work and come back to a result. I wouldn’t say that an experience feeling AGI-like means we’ve achieved AGI. But I think that ability to reason and act over many steps is a big part of what people are imagining when they think about it.

r001.rationale: The response describes asking AI to act, use a computer, and adjust, but does not say that watching Operator with o3 use a computer made AI feel AGI-like for many people.
